items.title: Tripartite Struggle — What, Why & Who
items.body:
### The contest for Kannauj

**In one line**
The Tripartite Struggle was a roughly two-century tug-of-war (8th–9th centuries) between three big dynasties for one north-Indian city, Kannauj.

**Why it is asked**
It explains why no single power ruled north India before the Turks arrived — a cause-and-effect favourite that links the fall of Harsha to the coming of the Delhi Sultanate.

**The story (a vacuum and a prize)**
When **Harsha's empire** broke up in the mid-7th century, north India was left with no overlord — several regional powers each wanted to be the new paramount ruler. Three of them clashed again and again over the city of **Kannauj**: the **Palas** of Bengal and Bihar in the east, the **Gurjara-Pratiharas** of Avanti in the centre-west, and the **Rashtrakutas** of the Deccan in the south. Because the fighting was three-sided it is called the **Tripartite ('three-party') Struggle**, or the Kannauj Triangle Wars. Kannauj mattered for hard and soft reasons alike: it sat on the busy **Ganga trade route** (so it brought market wealth), and as **Harsha's old capital** it carried huge prestige — whoever held it could claim to be the **'Lord of North India'**.

**Picture it (why Kannauj)**

| Motive | Explanation |
|---|---|
| Trade | On the Ganga route — a hub of rich markets |
| Legitimacy | Harsha's former capital; holding it conferred prestige |
| Money | Trade revenue funded armies and administration |
| Title | Winner claimed Sakalottarapathanatha / Uttarapathaswami ('Lord of North India') |

**Terms explained**
- **Tripartite:** 'three-party' — a contest among three sides.
- **Power vacuum:** a gap left when a strong central ruler disappears, inviting rivals to compete.
- **Sakalottarapathanatha / Uttarapathaswami:** titles meaning 'Lord/Master of the northern country'.

**Don't confuse**
- The Tripartite contenders (**Palas, Pratiharas, Rashtrakutas**) are not the Tamil 'three crowned kings' (**Cholas, Pandyas, Cheras**).
- **Kannauj** (the prize) is not **Thanesar**, which was Harsha's earlier seat before he moved to Kannauj.

**Remember it**
Three powers, one city: 'PPR fight for Kannauj' — **P**alas, **P**ratiharas, **R**ashtrakutas.

**TL;DR**
- Tripartite Struggle = Palas, Gurjara-Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas contesting Kannauj across the 8th–9th centuries.
- It arose from the power vacuum left by the decline of Harsha's empire.
- Kannauj was prized for its Ganga trade-route wealth and its legitimacy as Harsha's old capital.
- The winner claimed the title Sakalottarapathanatha / Uttarapathaswami — Lord of North India.

items.title: The Three Contenders at a Glance
items.body:
### The three rival dynasties

**In one line**
The three contenders were the Palas (east), the Gurjara-Pratiharas (centre-west) and the Rashtrakutas (Deccan) — each strong in its own base but reaching for Kannauj.

**Why it is asked**
Match-the-following and statement questions regularly test who founded each line, their peak ruler and their signature legacy.

**The story (three regional powers)**
The **Palas** rose in Bengal and Bihar around 750. Their founder **Gopala** was unusual — he was **elected** by local chiefs to end the anarchy (matsyanyaya, 'the law of the fish', where the strong eat the weak). His successors **Dharmapala** and **Devapala** made the Palas the great **Buddhist patrons of the east**: Dharmapala founded **Vikramshila University** and revived **Nalanda**. The **Gurjara-Pratiharas** rose from the **Mandor** region near Jodhpur; under **Mihira Bhoja** they reached their peak and are credited with **blocking the Arab advance** from Sindh, earning the epithet **'Ranahastina'** (lords of war). The **Rashtrakutas** of the Deccan, founded by **Dantidurga**, were the wild card: kings like Dhruva and **Govinda III** struck north and won battles, but revolts back home in the Deccan always forced them to withdraw, so they never kept Kannauj. Their lasting glory is the rock-cut **Kailasa temple at Ellora** and early Kannada literature.

**Picture it (compare the three)**

| Dynasty | Base | Founder | Peak ruler | Signature legacy |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pala | Bengal & Bihar | Gopala (elected) | Dharmapala / Devapala | Vikramshila; revived Nalanda; Buddhism |
| Gurjara-Pratihara | Avanti (from Mandor) | Nagabhata I | Mihira Bhoja | Checked the Arabs; 'Ranahastina' |
| Rashtrakuta | Deccan | Dantidurga | Govinda III | Kailasa temple, Ellora; Kannada literature |

**Terms explained**
- **Matsyanyaya:** 'the law of the fish' — lawless chaos where the strong devour the weak; the Palas were elected to end it.
- **Ranahastina:** 'war-elephant / lord of war', an epithet of the Pratiharas.
- **Vikramshila:** a famous Buddhist university founded by Dharmapala.

**Don't confuse**
- The Pratihara peak ruler **Mihira Bhoja** is different from the later Paramara scholar-king **Bhoja of Dhar**.
- The Palas' **elected** founder Gopala is a rare exception — most medieval kingship was hereditary.

**Remember it**
'PPR' contenders — **P**alas (east), **P**ratiharas (centre/west), **R**ashtrakutas (south). Palas = Buddhism, Pratiharas = anti-Arab shield, Rashtrakutas = Ellora.

**TL;DR**
- Pala founder Gopala was elected; Dharmapala founded Vikramshila and revived Nalanda.
- The Palas were the leading Buddhist patrons of Bengal and Bihar.
- Gurjara-Pratiharas rose from Mandor; Mihira Bhoja checked the Arabs and they were called 'Ranahastina'.
- Rashtrakutas were founded by Dantidurga and built the Kailasa temple at Ellora.
- Rashtrakuta Govinda III defeated the Pratihara Nagabhata II but could not hold Kannauj because of compulsions (trouble at home) in the Deccan.
keyPoints: Pala founder Gopala was elected; Dharmapala founded Vikramshila and revived Nalanda.
The Palas were the leading Buddhist patrons of Bengal and Bihar.
Gurjara-Pratiharas rose from Mandor; Mihira Bhoja checked the Arabs and they were called 'Ranahastina'.
Rashtrakutas were founded by Dantidurga and built the Kailasa temple at Ellora.
Govinda III defeated Nagabhata II but could not hold Kannauj because of Deccan compulsions.

items.title: Phases, Battles & Outcome
items.body:
### How the struggle unfolded

**In one line**
The struggle ran in two main phases; the Pratiharas eventually came out on top, but the long fighting left all three powers weak and north India divided.

**Why it is asked**
Examiners like the sequence of who-beat-whom and the big-picture consequence — fragmentation that opened the door to the Turks.

**The story (two rounds, no clear winner)**
In **Phase I (about 790–810)** the Pratihara king **Vatsaraja** beat the Pala king **Dharmapala** near Prayag, but was then crushed by the Rashtrakuta **Dhruva I**, who could not stay in the north because of trouble in the Deccan — so Kannauj kept changing hands. In **Phase II (about 810–836)** the Pratihara **Nagabhata II** captured Kannauj from **Chakrayudha**, a puppet ruler propped up by the Palas; the Rashtrakuta **Govinda III** then defeated Nagabhata II but again withdrew south. This pattern — the Rashtrakutas winning battles yet leaving — meant that by the **late 9th century the Pratiharas emerged as the leading power** in the north. But victory was costly. The endless wars **drained all three dynasties**, left **no lasting central authority**, and so the Pratihara empire slowly broke apart. Out of its pieces grew the independent **Rajput states**, which were later overrun by the **Ghurids**.

**Picture it (the two phases)**

| Phase | Key events |
|---|---|
| Phase I (c.790–810) | Vatsaraja beats Dharmapala, then loses to Dhruva |
| Phase II (c.810–836) | Nagabhata II takes Kannauj from Chakrayudha; Govinda III wins but withdraws |
| Result | Pratiharas dominant by late 9th c.; all three weakened |

**Terms explained**
- **Puppet ruler:** a king placed on a throne and controlled by a stronger outside power (here, Chakrayudha, backed by the Palas).
- **Fragmentation:** the breaking of one large state into many small independent ones.

**Don't confuse**
- **Vatsaraja and Nagabhata II** are both Pratihara kings of different phases — keep their battles separate.
- The Rashtrakutas **won several battles** but never **held** Kannauj — winning is not the same as keeping.

**Remember it**
Rashtrakutas = 'hit and run' from the Deccan; the **Pratiharas** stayed and so won the north — only to break up later into Rajput states.

**TL;DR**
- Phase I: Vatsaraja beat Dharmapala but lost to Dhruva; Kannauj kept changing hands.
- Phase II: Nagabhata II captured Kannauj from Chakrayudha (the Pala vassal); Govinda III won but withdrew to the Deccan.
- What they fought for: each contender sought the title **Sakalottarapathanatha**, 'Lord of North India'.
- The Pratiharas emerged as the leading northern power by the late 9th century.
- The struggle drained all three powers and left north India politically fragmented.
- Pratihara decline gave rise to independent Rajput states later overrun by the Ghurids.
keyPoints: Phase I: Vatsaraja beat Dharmapala but lost to Dhruva; Kannauj kept changing hands.
Phase II: Nagabhata II captured Kannauj from Chakrayudha; Govinda III won but withdrew to the Deccan.
The Pratiharas emerged as the leading northern power by the late 9th century.

items.title: Rise of the Rajput States after the Pratiharas
items.body:
### The Rajput successor states

**In one line**
When the Pratihara empire broke up, its feudatories became independent Rajput kingdoms famous for temple-building.

**Why it is asked**
Their monuments — Khajuraho, Modhera, Rani-ki-Vav — are high-value art-and-architecture facts, and their disunity is the standard explanation for the Turkish conquest.

**The story (feudatories become kings)**
As the Gurjara-Pratihara centre weakened in the 10th century, the chiefs who had served under it set up their own kingdoms. The **Chandellas** took **Jejakabhukti** (modern **Bundelkhand**); made sovereign by **Dhanga** and raised to their peak by **Vidyadhar** (who captured Kanauj in 1018), they built the celebrated **Khajuraho** temples, crowned by the **Kandariya Mahadev**. The **Paramaras** ruled **Malwa** from **Dharanagar (Dhar)**; their scholar-king **Bhoja** (1010–1055) founded **Bhojpur**, built the **Bhojeshwar Temple**, and wrote on philosophy and poetics. The **Chaulukyas (Solankis)** of Gujarat ruled from **Anhilawada (Patan)** and developed the graceful **Maru-Gurjara** style seen in the **Modhera Sun Temple** and the **Rani-ki-Vav** stepwell. It was during the Solanki **Bhimadeva I's** reign that **Mahmud of Ghazni plundered the Somnath Temple (1025)**.

**Picture it (dynasty → monument)**

| Dynasty | Region / capital | Peak ruler | Signature monument |
|---|---|---|---|
| Chandellas | Bundelkhand; Khajuraho/Kalanjara | Vidyadhar | Khajuraho (Kandariya Mahadev) |
| Paramaras | Malwa; Dhar | Bhoja | Bhojeshwar Temple, Bhojpur |
| Solankis | Gujarat; Patan | Jaisimha / Kumarpala | Modhera Sun Temple; Rani-ki-Vav |

**Terms explained**
- **Feudatory:** a lesser ruler serving a greater one; many became independent when the Pratiharas fell.
- **Maru-Gurjara:** the western-Indian temple style of Rajasthan and Gujarat (Solanki art).
- **Agnikula myth:** a legend tracing some Rajput clans to a fire-pit sacrifice at Mount Abu.

**Don't confuse**
- **Modhera Sun Temple (Solanki, Gujarat)** is not the **Konark Sun Temple** (Eastern Ganga, Odisha).
- **Bhoja the Paramara (Dhar)** is a different Bhoja from the Pratihara **Mihira Bhoja**.
- The **Kailasa temple, Ellora** belongs to the **Rashtrakutas** of the Deccan, not to any Rajput state — a common odd-one-out in dynasty–monument matches.

**Remember it**
Dynasty-to-temple: **Chandella = Khajuraho**, **Paramara = Bhojpur**, **Solanki = Modhera & Rani-ki-Vav**.

**TL;DR**
- Chandellas ruled Jejakabhukti (Bundelkhand) and built Khajuraho, including the Kandariya Mahadev temple.
- Paramara Bhoja ruled from Dharanagar (Dhar), founded Bhojpur and built the Bhojeshwar Temple; a scholar-king, he also authored works on philosophy, poetics and architecture.
- Solankis (Chaulukyas) of Gujarat ruled from Anhilawada (Patan) and built the Modhera Sun Temple and Rani-ki-Vav.
- Somnath was plundered by Mahmud of Ghazni under Bhimadeva I in 1025 CE.
- The agnikula myth derives several Rajput clans from a fire-pit sacrifice at Mount Abu.
keyPoints: Chandellas ruled Jejakabhukti (Bundelkhand) and built Khajuraho, including the Kandariya Mahadev temple.
Paramara Bhoja ruled from Dharanagar (Dhar) and built Bhojpur and the Bhojeshwar Temple.
Solankis (Chaulukyas) of Gujarat ruled from Anhilawada (Patan) and built the Modhera Sun Temple and Rani-ki-Vav.
Somnath was plundered by Mahmud of Ghazni under Bhimadeva I in 1025 CE.
The agnikula myth derives several Rajput clans from a fire-pit sacrifice at Mount Abu.

items.title: Chauhans, Gahadavalas, Tomaras & the Tarain Battles
items.body:
### The last Rajput powers before the Sultanate

**In one line**
The Chauhans, Gahadavalas and Tomaras were the final Rajput powers of the north; their defeat at Tarain (1192) and Chandawar (1194) opened India to Turkish rule.

**Why it is asked**
The two Battles of Tarain are among the most asked dates in medieval history, and the disunity of these Rajputs is the textbook cause of the Delhi Sultanate.

**The story (three kingdoms and two battles)**
The **Tomaras** ruled around Delhi (Dhillika) from the 10th century; **Anangpal Tomar** built the fort of **Lal Kot**. Delhi later passed to the **Chauhans (Chahmanas) of Ajmer**, who had begun as Pratihara feudatories; **Ajayaraja** founded the city of **Ajmer**, and **Prithviraj III (Rai Pithora)** became the most famous Chauhan king. To the east, the **Gahadavalas** held **Kannauj and Varanasi** (1090–1193), reaching their peak under **Govindachandra**, with **Jaichandra** as the last great ruler. The crisis came from the north-west, where **Muhammad Ghori** was expanding. At the **First Battle of Tarain (1191)** Prithviraj III **defeated** Ghori; but at the **Second Battle of Tarain (1192)** Ghori returned and **defeated** Prithviraj, shattering Chauhan power. Two years later **Jaichandra** was defeated and killed by the Ghurids at **Chandawar (1194)**, and Kannauj too fell to Turkish rule.

**Picture it (the Tarain battles)**

| Battle | Year | Result |
|---|---|---|
| First Tarain | 1191 CE | Prithviraj III defeats Muhammad Ghori |
| Second Tarain | 1192 CE | Ghori defeats Prithviraj — Chauhan power collapses |
| Chandawar | 1194 CE | Ghori defeats and kills Jaichandra Gahadavala |

**Terms explained**
- **Lal Kot:** the earliest fortified city of Delhi, built by the Tomaras.
- **Prithviraj Raso:** a later epic poem by Chand Bardai; dramatic but historically unreliable. It claims Jaichandra invited Muhammad Ghori, but no inscription confirms this.
- **Agnikula myth:** a legend tracing certain Rajput clans to a fire-pit sacrifice at Mount Abu.
- **Prithviraj Vijaya:** a contemporary Sanskrit work by Jayanaka; the more reliable source.

**Don't confuse**
- **First Tarain (1191) = Prithviraj wins**; **Second Tarain (1192) = Ghori wins**. The second battle is the decisive one.
- **Jaichandra Gahadavala** was defeated at **Chandawar (1194)**, not at Tarain.

**Remember it**
Tarain: ''91 Prithviraj, '92 Ghori' — the loser of the second battle lost India; Jaichandra fell at Chandawar in '94.

**TL;DR**
- Anangpal Tomar built Lal Kot at Delhi; the Chauhans later took Delhi.
- Chauhan Ajayaraja founded Ajmer; Prithviraj III was the most famous Chauhan king.
- First Battle of Tarain (1191): Prithviraj wins; Second Battle of Tarain (1192): Ghori wins.
- Gahadavala Govindachandra brought the dynasty to its peak; Jaichandra died fighting the Ghurids in 1194.
- Prithviraj Vijaya (Jayanaka) is reliable; Prithviraj Raso (Chand Bardai) is a later, unverified account.
keyPoints: Anangpal Tomar built Lal Kot at Delhi; the Chauhans later took Delhi.
Chauhan Ajayaraja founded Ajmer; Prithviraj III was the most famous Chauhan king.
First Battle of Tarain (1191): Prithviraj wins; Second Battle of Tarain (1192): Ghori wins.
Gahadavala Govindachandra brought the dynasty to its peak; Jaichandra died fighting the Ghurids in 1194.
Prithviraj Vijaya (Jayanaka) is reliable; Prithviraj Raso (Chand Bardai) is a later, unverified account.

items.title: The Palas of Bengal — Monasteries, Kings and Sources
items.body:
### The Palas of Bengal — Monasteries, Kings and Sources

**In one line**
The Palas (c.750–1160s) were the eastern contender for Kannauj and the last great royal patrons of Buddhism in India; exams ask their monasteries, their zenith under Devapala and their links with South-East Asia and Tibet.

**The story**
After **Gopala** was chosen king to end the anarchy, the early Palas founded **Odantapuri**. **Dharmapala** held a grand assembly at Kannauj (the **Khalimpur** plate), built **Vikramshila** and the **Somapura Mahavihara** at **Paharpur**, and called himself **Paramasaugata**. **Devapala** took the empire to its **zenith** and granted villages to a Nalanda monastery built by the Sailendra king **Balaputradeva**. Later, **Mahipala I** revived the dynasty but lost to **Rajendra Chola**, **Ramapala** crushed the **Kaivarta** revolt (the **Ramacharita**), and **Atisha** carried Pala Buddhism to Tibet. The **Senas** replaced the Palas in the 12th century.

#### Pala facts

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Odantapuri** | Monastery at Bihar Sharif founded under the early Palas (traditionally Gopala); model for Tibet's Samye |
| **Somapura Mahavihara** | Built by Dharmapala at **Paharpur** (now Bangladesh); UNESCO site (1985) |
| **Khalimpur copper plate** | Describes Dharmapala's darbar at Kannauj installing Chakrayudha, attended by many northern kings |
| **Paramasaugata** | Dharmapala's title — 'supreme follower of the Buddha'; he also claimed to be Uttarapathaswamin |
| **Devapala** | c.810–850; **zenith** of the Pala empire (Assam to the Vindhyas) |
| **Balaputradeva** | Sailendra king of Suvarnadvipa (Sumatra/Java) who built a Nalanda monastery; Devapala granted it five villages |
| **Mahipala I** | c.988–1038; revived the Palas; defeated by **Rajendra Chola** (1022) |
| **Ramapala** | Recovered Varendra after the **Kaivarta** revolt (Divya); story told in Sandhyakara Nandi's **Ramacharita** |
| **Atisha Dipankara** | Teacher of Vikramshila who went to Tibet (1040s) and revived Buddhism there |
| **Pala art** | Black basalt and bronze icons; illustrated **palm-leaf** Buddhist manuscripts (e.g. Prajnaparamita) |
| **End** | The **Senas** (Vijayasena) replaced the Palas in Bengal in the 12th century (the PDF ends Pala rule in 1161) |
| **Ruhmi** | Sulaiman's (851) name for the Pala kingdom, which he said had a large army |

**Don't confuse**
- **Vikramshila** and **Somapura** were founded by Dharmapala; **Nalanda** was older (Gupta age) and only revived by him.
- **Mahipala I** (Pala) lost to Rajendra Chola; **Mahipala** (Pratihara) lost Kannauj to Indra III — two different kings.

**TL;DR**
- Odantapuri (early Palas); Somapura at Paharpur (Dharmapala); Khalimpur plate.
- Devapala = zenith; Balaputradeva's Nalanda monastery.
- Mahipala I lost to Rajendra Chola; Ramacharita on the Kaivarta revolt; Atisha to Tibet; Senas replaced the Palas.
keyPoints: Dharmapala built the Somapura Mahavihara at Paharpur (UNESCO); the Khalimpur plate records his Kannauj assembly.
Devapala took the Palas to their zenith and endowed the Nalanda monastery of the Sailendra king Balaputradeva.
Mahipala I revived the Palas but lost to Rajendra Chola; Sandhyakara Nandi's Ramacharita tells of Ramapala and the Kaivarta revolt.
Atisha Dipankara of Vikramshila took Buddhism to Tibet; Pala art = black-stone icons and palm-leaf painting.
The Senas replaced the Palas in Bengal in the 12th century.

items.title: The Gurjara-Pratiharas — Kings, Titles and Foreign Witnesses
items.body:
### The Gurjara-Pratiharas — Kings, Titles and Foreign Witnesses

**In one line**
The Pratiharas (c.730–1036) won the Kannauj struggle in the long run; exams ask who founded the line, who made Kannauj the capital, the Adivaraha title, the court poet Rajashekhara and the king who fled from Mahmud.

**The story**
**Nagabhata I** founded the imperial line at Avanti and stopped the **Arabs**. **Vatsaraja** beat Dharmapala but lost to **Dhruva**. **Nagabhata II** took Kannauj and made it the **capital**. **Mihira Bhoja** ruled the empire at its height and put **Adivaraha** on his coins; the Arab **Sulaiman** praised Pratihara **cavalry**. **Mahendrapala I** kept the poet **Rajashekhara**, and **al-Masudi** visited under Mahipala. In **1018** the last major king, **Rajyapala**, fled before Mahmud of Ghazni and was killed by the Chandellas. The name **Pratihara** means **doorkeeper**, after **Lakshmana**.

#### Pratihara rulers and sources

| Ruler / source | Period | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Nagabhata I** | c.730–760 | Founder of the imperial line at Avanti (Ujjain); repulsed the **Arabs** of Sind |
| **Vatsaraja** | c.775–800 | Beat Dharmapala; then lost to the Rashtrakuta **Dhruva** (Phase I) |
| **Nagabhata II** | c.800–833 | Took Kannauj from Chakrayudha and made it the Pratihara **capital**; beat Dharmapala near Monghyr; lost to Govinda III |
| **Mihira Bhoja** (Bhoja I) | c.836–885 | Peak of the empire; title **Adivaraha** (Vishnu's boar form) on his coins; also 'Prabhasa' |
| **Sulaiman** (851) | — | Called the Pratihara (Juzr) king the strongest foe of the Arabs, with the finest **cavalry** in India |
| **Mahendrapala I** | c.885–910 | Patron of **Rajashekhara** (Karpuramanjari, Kavyamimamsa, Balaramayana) |
| **Mahipala** | c.912–944 | Visited by **al-Masudi** (915–16); lost Kannauj briefly to the Rashtrakuta Indra III (916) |
| **Rajyapala** | d.1019 | Fled Kannauj when **Mahmud** of Ghazni attacked (**1018**); killed by the Chandella Vidyadhara for cowardice |
| **Gwalior Prashasti** | — | Mihira Bhoja's eulogy — the main source for the Pratiharas |
| **Name** | — | Pratihara = '**doorkeeper**'; they claimed descent from **Lakshmana**, doorkeeper to Rama |

**Don't confuse**
- **Mihira Bhoja** (Pratihara, Adivaraha) ≠ **Bhoja** of Dhar (Paramara, 11th century).
- **Nagabhata I** fought the Arabs; **Nagabhata II** took Kannauj.
- **Sulaiman** (851) wrote about both the Pratiharas and the Rashtrakutas; **al-Masudi** came in 915–16.

**TL;DR**
- Nagabhata I founded the line and repulsed the Arabs; Nagabhata II made Kannauj the capital.
- Mihira Bhoja — Adivaraha; Sulaiman praised Pratihara cavalry.
- Rajashekhara — court of Mahendrapala I; al-Masudi visited (915–16).
- Rajyapala fled from Mahmud (1018).
keyPoints: Nagabhata I founded the imperial Pratiharas at Avanti and repulsed the Arabs; Nagabhata II made Kannauj the capital.
Mihira Bhoja took the title Adivaraha; his Gwalior Prashasti is the chief source.
Rajashekhara (Karpuramanjari, Kavyamimamsa) was the court poet of Mahendrapala I.
Rajyapala fled Kannauj before Mahmud of Ghazni in 1018.
Pratihara means doorkeeper — they claimed descent from Lakshmana.

items.title: Chandellas & Paramaras — Rulers, Temples, Books
items.body:
### Chandellas & Paramaras — Rulers, Temples, Books

**In one line**
The Chandellas (Bundelkhand) and Paramaras (Malwa) are asked through their founders, a few great kings, the Khajuraho temples and Bhoja's learning.

**The story**
The Chandellas began with **Nannuka**, a Pratihara feudatory. **Yashovarman** built the **Lakshmana temple**, **Dhanga** became sovereign and built the **Vishvanatha**, and **Vidyadhara** — who resisted Mahmud — is credited with the **Kandariya** Mahadeva. **Kirtivarman**'s court saw the play **Prabodhachandrodaya**, and **Paramardi**'s generals **Alha** and **Udal** died fighting Prithviraj. Khajuraho became a UNESCO site in **1986**. The Paramaras of Malwa rose under **Upendra**; **Siyaka** sacked **Manyakheta** (972), **Vakpati Munja** was killed by **Tailapa II**, and **Bhoja** built the **Bhoj Tal** and **Bhoj Shala** and wrote the **Samarangana Sutradhara**. Alauddin's army ended the line in **1305**.

#### Chandellas of Jejakabhukti

| Ruler / item | Period | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Nannuka** | c.831–845 | Founder; a Pratihara feudatory at Khajuraho |
| **Yashovarman** | c.925–950 | Built the **Lakshmana temple** (Vishnu), Khajuraho (inscription 954) |
| **Dhanga** | 950–999 | Declared sovereignty; ruled to the Betwa and Yamuna; built the **Vishvanatha** temple |
| **Vidyadhara** | 1003–1035 | Resisted Mahmud of Ghazni; built the **Kandariya** Mahadeva temple (the inscription names "Virimda", taken to be him) |
| **Kirtivarman** | 1060–1100 | Krishna Mishra's allegorical drama **Prabodhachandrodaya** was staged before him; after him the Kalachuris overran the kingdom |
| **Paramardi** | 1165–1203 | Generals **Alha** and **Udal** fell at Mahoba (1182) against Prithviraj; Aibak took Kalinjar (1202–03) |
| **Capitals** | — | Khajuraho, **Kalinjar** (Kalanjara) and **Mahoba** |
| **Khajuraho** | — | UNESCO site (**1986**); about 25 of an original **85** temples survive — Hindu and Jain, in the Nagara style |

#### Paramaras of Malwa

| Ruler / item | Period | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Upendra** (Krishnaraja) | 9th c. | Founder; a vassal set up by the Rashtrakutas to counter the Pratiharas |
| **Siyaka** | 940–972 | First independent Paramara; sacked **Manyakheta** in **972**, hastening the Rashtrakuta fall |
| **Vakpati Munja** | 972–995 | Poet-king; patron of Padmagupta and Dhanapala; captured and killed by the Chalukya **Tailapa II** |
| **Bhoja** | 1010–1055 | Built the **Bhoj Tal** (Bhopal lake) and the **Bhoj Shala** (Sanskrit college / Saraswati temple) at Dhar |
| **Samarangana Sutradhara** | — | Bhoja's treatise on architecture (vastu); he also wrote the Saraswati Kanthabharana and Rajamartanda |
| **Titles** | — | **Kaviraja**; Parameshwara-**Parambhattaraka** |
| **Triple alliance** | — | With **Rajendra Chola** and the **Kalachuri**s against the Western Chalukyas |
| **Sources** | — | **Udaipur Prashasti** and Nagpur Prashasti; Harsola copper plates (Siyaka as Rashtrakuta feudatory) |
| **End** | 1305 | **Alauddin** Khalji's army killed the last ruler, Mahalakadeva, and took Malwa |

**Don't confuse**
- **Lakshmana temple** (Yashovarman) and **Kandariya Mahadeva** (Vidyadhara) are both at Khajuraho; tie each to its king.
- **Siyaka** sacked Manyakheta (972); **Tailapa II** then ended the Rashtrakutas (973) and later killed **Munja**.

**TL;DR**
- Nannuka → Yashovarman (Lakshmana) → Dhanga (Vishvanatha) → Vidyadhara (Kandariya) → Kirtivarman → Paramardi (Alha-Udal).
- Khajuraho UNESCO 1986.
- Siyaka sacked Manyakheta (972); Munja killed by Tailapa II; Bhoja — Bhoj Tal, Bhoj Shala, Samarangana Sutradhara; end 1305.
keyPoints: Nannuka founded the Chandellas; Yashovarman built the Lakshmana temple; Dhanga built the Vishvanatha temple.
The Kandariya Mahadeva temple is attributed to Vidyadhara; Khajuraho became a UNESCO site in 1986.
Alha and Udal, Paramardi's generals, died at Mahoba (1182); Prabodhachandrodaya was staged under Kirtivarman.
Paramara Siyaka sacked Manyakheta (972); Vakpati Munja was killed by Tailapa II.
Bhoja: Bhoj Tal (Bhopal), Bhoj Shala (Dhar), Samarangana Sutradhara; the Paramaras ended in 1305.

items.title: Solankis, Tomaras, Chauhans & Gahadavalas — the Details
items.body:
### Solankis, Tomaras, Chauhans & Gahadavalas — the Details

**In one line**
The western and northern Rajput dynasties are asked through Dilwara and Rani-ki-Vav, Hemachandra, Ghori's first defeat (1178), the founding of Ajmer, and the poets of Prithviraj and Jaichandra.

**The story**
In Gujarat **Mularaja I** founded the Solanki kingdom at Anhilwara. Under **Bhima I** came Mahmud's sack of Somnath, the **Vimal Vasahi** temple at **Dilwara**, and Queen **Udayamati**'s **Rani-ki-Vav**. **Jayasimha Siddharaja** and **Kumarapala** patronised **Hemachandra**, and in **1178** a Solanki army led by **Naikidevi** gave Muhammad Ghori his first defeat. The **Vaghelas** followed, and **Karna** lost Gujarat to Alauddin. Around Delhi the **Tomaras** founded **Dhillika**; **Ajayaraja** founded **Ajmer**, **Vigraharaja IV** took Delhi and wrote the **Harakeli** Nataka, and **Jayanaka** praised Prithviraj III. In the Ganga valley **Chandradeva** founded the Gahadavalas, **Lakshmidhara** compiled the **Kritya Kalpataru**, and **Shri Harsha** wrote at Jaichandra's court.

#### Chaulukyas (Solankis) and Vaghelas of Gujarat

| Ruler / item | Period | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Mularaja I** | c.940–995 | Founder; capital **Anhilwara** (Patan) |
| **Bhima I** | 1022–1064 | Somnath sacked by Mahmud (1025); Modhera Sun temple (1026); minister Vimala built **Vimal Vasahi**, **Dilwara** (1031) |
| **Rani-ki-Vav** | — | Stepwell built by Queen **Udayamati** for Bhima I; UNESCO **2014**; on the new ₹100 note |
| **Jayasimha Siddharaja** | 1092–1142 | Annexed Malwa; patron of the Jain scholar **Hemachandra** (Siddha-Hema grammar); built the Rudra Mahalaya at Siddhpur |
| **Kumarapala** | 1143–1172 | Adopted **Jainism** under Hemachandra; stern with rebels |
| **Mularaja II / Bhima II** | 1178 | Ghori's first defeat in India — at Kayadara near Mount Abu (**1178**), by an army led by queen-mother **Naikidevi** |
| **Fall of Anhilwara** | 1197 | Sacked by **Qutb-ud-din Aibak** (the PDF calls it Naharwala) |
| **Vaghelas** | 1240s–1299 | Usurped Solanki power; **Karna** Vaghela lost Gujarat to Alauddin (1299) |
| **Luna Vasahi**, Dilwara | 1230 | Built by the ministers Vastupala and **Tejapala** |

#### Tomaras, Chauhans and Gahadavalas

| Ruler / item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Tomaras** | Founded **Dhillika** (Delhi) — traditionally **736**, Anangpal I; Anangpal II built Lal Kot (11th c.) |
| **Tomara sources** | Gwalior manuscript (**Khadag Rai**), Ain-i-Akbari, Kumaon manuscript |
| **Hansi** (Anshika) | Anangpal built the Asigarh fort here, a centre for fine **swords** |
| **Ajayaraja** | Founded **Ajayameru** (Ajmer) as the Chauhan capital (c.1113) |
| **Arnoraja** | Built the **Anasagar** lake at Ajmer; married the daughter of the Solanki Jayasimha |
| **Vigraharaja IV** (Visaladeva) | Took Delhi from the Tomaras (c.1152); wrote **Harakeli** Nataka; built a Sanskrit college at Ajmer (later the Adhai Din ka Jhonpra) |
| **Prithviraj III** | '**Rai Pithora**'; c.1177–1192; enlarged Lal Kot into **Qila Rai Pithora**; came to the throne aged eleven |
| **Tarain** | **Taraori**, near Karnal–Thanesar in **Haryana** |
| **Jayanaka** | **Prithviraja Vijaya** (Sanskrit) — reliable; full Chauhan genealogy; ends before the Second Battle of Tarain |
| **Chandradeva** | Founded Gahadavala rule at Kannauj; made Varanasi a second capital |
| **Govindachandra** | Peak (1114–1155; Monghyr to Delhi); minister **Lakshmidhara** compiled the **Kritya Kalpataru**; queen Kumaradevi built a vihara at Sarnath |
| **Jaichandra** | Last great Gahadavala (1170–1194); the poet **Shri Harsha** wrote the **Naishadhacharita** at his court |
| **Turushkadanda** | A Gahadavala tax — read as a levy to pay off (or a tax on) the Turks |
| **Ibn al-Athir** | Kamil-ut-Tawarikh: Jaichandra ruled the **largest** kingdom among the Rajputs |
| **Harishchandra** | Jaichandra's son held Kannauj and Varanasi (Kotwa inscription) until **Iltutmish** took Kannauj |

**Don't confuse**
- **Kayadara (1178)**: Ghori defeated by the Solankis — his first defeat in India; **First Tarain (1191)**: defeated by Prithviraj.
- **Prithviraja Vijaya** (Jayanaka, Sanskrit, reliable) ≠ **Prithviraj Raso** (Chand Bardai, later, legendary).
- **Vimal Vasahi** (1031, Vimala) and **Luna Vasahi** (1230, Vastupala–Tejapala) are both at Dilwara, Mount Abu.

**TL;DR**
- Mularaja I founded the Solankis; Bhima I — Somnath sack, Modhera, Vimal Vasahi; Udayamati — Rani-ki-Vav (UNESCO 2014).
- Hemachandra under Jayasimha and Kumarapala; Kayadara 1178 — Ghori beaten; Aibak sacked Anhilwara 1197.
- Ajayaraja founded Ajmer; Vigraharaja IV — Harakeli Nataka; Jayanaka — Prithviraja Vijaya.
- Gahadavalas: Chandradeva; Lakshmidhara's Kritya Kalpataru; Shri Harsha's Naishadhacharita; Turushkadanda tax.
keyPoints: Vimal Vasahi (Dilwara, 1031) was built by Vimala Shah, minister of Bhima I; Rani-ki-Vav by Queen Udayamati (UNESCO 2014).
Hemachandra flourished under Jayasimha Siddharaja and Kumarapala; Kumarapala adopted Jainism.
Muhammad Ghori was first defeated in India in 1178 near Mount Abu by the Solankis (queen-mother Naikidevi).
Ajayaraja founded Ajmer; Vigraharaja IV took Delhi and wrote Harakeli Nataka; Jayanaka wrote the Prithviraja Vijaya.
Shri Harsha wrote the Naishadhacharita at Jaichandra's court; Lakshmidhara compiled the Kritya Kalpataru; the Gahadavalas levied Turushkadanda.

items.title: Tripartite Phases in Detail, Lesser Dynasties and Rajput Origins
items.body:
### Tripartite Phases in Detail, Lesser Dynasties and Rajput Origins

**In one line**
This note fills in the battle sites and titles of the Tripartite Struggle, the smaller dynasties of the period, and the debate on Rajput origins.

**The story**
The struggle opened near **Prayag**, where Vatsaraja beat Dharmapala; the Rashtrakuta Dhruva then beat both and added the **Ganga and Yamuna** to his emblem. Kannauj itself — **Kanyakubja** or **Mahodaya** — was ruled by the weak **Ayudha** kings. In Phase II Nagabhata II beat Dharmapala near **Monghyr**. After about **two centuries** the Pratiharas were the **leading power** of the north. Around them stood smaller dynasties: the **Kalachuris** of **Tripuri**, the **Kachchhapaghatas** of Gwalior and the **Hindushahis** of **Waihind**. Later bards traced four Rajput clans to a fire-pit on Mount Abu, while **Tod** argued for foreign roots.

#### Phases, sites and titles

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Prayag** | Phase I (c.790–810) opened with Vatsaraja (Pratihara) defeating Dharmapala (Pala) near **Prayag** |
| **Ganga–Yamuna emblem** | Dhruva added the **Ganga and Yamuna** to the Rashtrakuta insignia after his northern victory |
| **Ayudha kings** | **Indrayudha**, Vajrayudha and Chakrayudha — weak rulers of Kannauj; Dharmapala replaced Indrayudha with Chakrayudha |
| **Monghyr** | Phase II: Nagabhata II defeated Dharmapala near **Monghyr** (Mungir, Bihar) |
| **Names of Kannauj** | **Kanyakubja** and **Mahodaya**; on the Ganga trade route; Harsha's old capital |
| **Duration** | About **two centuries** (8th to 10th c.); sharpest phase c.785–816 |
| **Uttarapathaswami** | 'Lord of the Northern Region' — claimed alongside Sakalottarapathanatha |
| **Winner** | The Pratiharas emerged as the **leading power** of the north by the end of the 9th century |
| **Bhasarvajna** | Logician; author of the Nyayasara |

#### Lesser dynasties and Rajput origins

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Kalachuris of Tripuri** | Near Jabalpur; Gangeyadeva and **Lakshmikarna** (Karna) were their great kings |
| **Kachchhapaghatas** | Rulers of Gwalior; built the **Sas-Bahu** temple (1093) |
| **Hindushahis** | Capital **Waihind** (Udabhandapur); **Jayapala** and Anandapala resisted Sabuktigin and Mahmud |
| **Agnikula clans** | Pratiharas, **Chauhan**s, Chaulukyas (**Solanki**s) and **Paramara**s — from Vasishtha's fire-pit on Mount Abu (told in the Prithviraj Raso) |
| **Origin debate** | Colonial writers like James **Tod** saw foreign roots (Sakas, **Hunas**, Gurjaras); Indian scholars stress indigenous Kshatriya descent |

**Don't confuse**
- **Prayag** = Phase I (Vatsaraja beat Dharmapala); **Monghyr** = Phase II (Nagabhata II beat Dharmapala).
- **Hindushahis** (Waihind, Punjab) fought Mahmud; they are not Rajputs of the Agnikula list.

**TL;DR**
- Prayag (Phase I), Monghyr (Phase II); Ayudha kings of Kannauj; Ganga–Yamuna emblem (Dhruva).
- Pratiharas the leading power by c.900.
- Kalachuris (Tripuri), Kachchhapaghatas (Sas-Bahu), Hindushahis (Waihind).
- Agnikula: Pratihara, Chauhan, Solanki, Paramara; Tod — foreign origin.
keyPoints: Phase I opened with Vatsaraja defeating Dharmapala near Prayag; in Phase II Nagabhata II beat Dharmapala near Monghyr.
Indrayudha, Vajrayudha and Chakrayudha were the weak Ayudha kings of Kannauj (also called Kanyakubja or Mahodaya).
By the end of the 9th century the Pratiharas were the leading power; the winner claimed Uttarapathaswami / Sakalottarapathanatha.
Kalachuris ruled from Tripuri; Kachchhapaghatas built the Sas-Bahu temple; the Hindushahis ruled from Waihind.
Agnikula clans: Pratiharas, Chauhans, Solankis, Paramaras.

items.title: For Mains — Kanauj & the Tripartite Struggle
items.body:
### For Mains — Kanauj & the Tripartite Struggle

Mains clause **M2-1b** (paper **mains-2**) places this topic with the Guptas, Kanauj and post-Harsha India. The analytical question is almost always *cause → course → consequence*, and why the north was divided when the Turks came.

**Dimensions Mains asks**

| Dimension | What to write |
| --- | --- |
| Causes | Post-Harsha vacuum; Kannauj's trade (Ganga route) and legitimacy value |
| Course | Phase I (Vatsaraja–Dharmapala–Dhruva); Phase II (Nagabhata II–Chakrayudha; Govinda III) |
| Consequences | Exhaustion of all three; political fragmentation; rise of Rajput states |
| Significance | Pratihara shield against the Arabs; cultural flowering amid conflict |
| Link to Sultanate | Disunity eased Ghaznavid raids and the Ghurid conquest (Tarain 1192) |
| Criticism | 'Pratihara as bulwark' thesis is debated; outcomes were regional, not total collapse |

**Evidence to quote**
- Imperial titles Sakalottarapathanatha / Uttarapathaswami — the symbolic value of Kannauj.
- Pala patronage of Nalanda and the founding of Vikramshila (Dharmapala) — a cultural counterpoint to the warfare.
- Rashtrakuta Kailasa temple at Ellora and Kavirajamarga — Deccan achievements despite northern raids.
- Mahmud of Ghazni's 17 raids (including Somnath, 1025) and the Second Battle of Tarain (1192) — the cost of disunity.
- Historians: R. S. Sharma and the 'Indian feudalism' thesis on political fragmentation.

**AP / wider-India angle**
The Rashtrakuta leg of the struggle ties the Deccan directly to north-Indian politics, and Rashtrakuta patronage seeded Kannada literature — a reminder that 'national' history ran through the south too.

**Use in answers**
- Example to cite: contrast the political fragmentation with the simultaneous cultural creativity (temples, universities) to show a nuanced, non-'dark age' view.
- Quote: the 'Lord of North India' title to show that Kannauj was a symbol of paramountcy, not just a city.
- Diagram idea: a triangle map placing Palas (east), Pratiharas (centre), Rashtrakutas (south) around Kannauj, with arrows for each phase.
keyPoints: Mains M2-1b (mains-2): structure answers as cause → course → consequence around Kannauj.
Causes: post-Harsha vacuum + Kannauj's trade and legitimacy value.
Consequence: exhaustion and fragmentation, producing the Rajput states.
Link to the Sultanate: disunity eased the Ghaznavid raids and the Ghurid conquest (Tarain 1192).
Nuance line: cultural flowering (Vikramshila, Ellora) alongside political division — avoid the 'dark age' label.
Cite R. S. Sharma's 'Indian feudalism' thesis and debate the 'Pratihara bulwark against the Arabs' claim.
